tools.name: search
description: Find documents whose text is about something: keyword and meaning search over the text of every document (and the common field values shown with it).

When to call it: the answer is written in a document's text (a message, a description, a transcript), or you know words but not which field holds them. To narrow it, give a source, a created range, or within= a result set from filter or lookup_key: only those documents are ranked, so nothing in the set is missed for being outside a global top list.
Example: search(query="why the release was delayed", source="<source>", created_from="2024-03", created_to="2024-04")

How the words match (case does not matter): text in double quotes is one exact phrase (its words together, in that order), and so is a key or code written with - _ / . or # (XY-123 matches 'XY-123' or 'XY 123', never XY-1234 or a lone 123); every other word matches on its own. Any part may match, and documents with more of the parts rank first (OR and AND are not needed: they are not searched for). Example: search(query="\"an exact phrase\" XY-123 other words"). Meaning search runs beside it on the whole query.

What comes back: 8 documents, best first (D# handle, source, created date, title), each with its best passages, and a paging line: 'documents 1-8; next: offset=8' while more follow and are not counted yet, 'documents 9-16 of 20; next: offset=16' once every document in scope is ranked, '(last page)' at the end. Call again with that offset for the next 8: each later page searches deeper, so paging goes on until nothing in scope is left. A document marked 'meaning only' contains none of the words, phrases or keys (meaning search found it). If no document in scope contains them, the line after the first says so: then no document's text holds that phrase or key (a key may still be in a field: lookup_key finds it). read_document reads a whole document. For every document with a field value, and for exact counts, use filter instead.

query.description: What to look for: plain words, an exact phrase in double quotes, keys as written (names, keys and phrases help).

source.description: Search only this source (a name from the source list).

created_from.description: Only documents created on or after this date: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY.

created_to.description: Only documents created on or before this date (inclusive): YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY.

within.description: Search only the documents of this result-set handle (R#), from filter or lookup_key.

offset.description: Where the page starts, from the paging line of an earlier call. Default 0.

tools.name: filter
description: Find every document of one source whose fields meet all the conditions, with the exact count.

When to call it: 'which', 'how many', 'list all', or any question that names a field value (a status, a person, a priority, a date, an amount, a team, a company). Field values that are not in a document's text can only be found this way. The source list and list_fields show each source's fields.

Ops: eq (value), in (values), contains (value: part of the text), range (from and/or to, inclusive: numbers, or dates YYYY-MM-DD / YYYY-MM / YYYY), present, missing (no value: empty or absent). Values match loosely (case, spaces and punctuation do not matter); persons match however they are written; each item of a list field is matched on its own. eq on a date field means that day (or month, or year). created_from / created_to match the document's own created date. A date outside the corpus's date window counts as no date: no date range matches it, and the result says how many documents that leaves out.
Example: filter(source="<source>", conditions=[{"field": "<field>", "op": "eq", "value": "open"}, {"field": "<date field>", "op": "range", "from": "2024-01", "to": "2024-03"}])

What comes back: the exact number of matches, an R# handle holding every match (newest first: cite it to cite them all, give it to read_fields or search within=), what each value matched, how many documents of the source have each field with a value, empty, or not at all, and 50 rows at a time ('rows 1-50 of 278; next: offset=50'). Call again with that offset for the next rows, or add a condition. If a value matches nothing, or several spellings, an error lists the real values: pick from them.

source.description: The source to filter (a name from the source list).

conditions.description: Conditions, all of which must hold (AND). Empty: every document of the source (with the created range, if given).

field.description: A field of the source, exactly as list_fields or the source list shows it (the title field too).

value.description: For eq and contains: one value.

values.description: For in: the values, any of which may match.

from.description: For range: the lowest value, inclusive (a number or a date).

to.description: For range: the highest value, inclusive (a number or a date).

created_from.description: Only documents created on or after this date: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY.

created_to.description: Only documents created on or before this date (inclusive): YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY.

offset.description: Where the rows start, from the paging line of an earlier call. Default 0.

tools.name: read_fields
description: Read chosen field values of many documents at once, straight from the index.
When to call it: after filter or lookup_key, to say which ones and a detail of each (who owns each, when each was closed); or to compare a field across documents you were shown.
Example: read_fields(documents=["R1"], fields=["<field>", "<other field>"])

What comes back: one row per document (D#, source, created date, title, then each field's value; '(empty)', '(absent)', '(in the document text)' or '(not a field of source ...)' when it has none), 50 rows at a time with a paging line; call again with the offset for the next rows.

documents.description: Handles: R# for a whole result set, D# for one document.

fields.description: Field names, as list_fields or the source list shows them.

offset.description: Where the rows start, from the paging line of an earlier call. Default 0.

tools.name: read_document
description: Read one whole document: its facts, every field and its full text.
When to call it: a passage, row or title looks relevant and you need the exact wording, the context, or a detail the passage does not show.
Example: read_document(document="D3")
What comes back: the document's handle, source, created and updated dates, title, every field with its values, and the whole text, nothing left out.

document.description: A D# handle from an earlier result.

tools.name: lookup_key
description: Find a record by its own identifier (a ticket key, a record number, an id), and every document that refers to it.
When to call it: the question or a result names an identifier and you need its record, or what links to it.
Example: lookup_key(key="<KEY-123>")

What comes back: the documents that own the key, then the documents that refer to it in a field (with the field and value), as an R# handle and rows with a paging line. Mentions of the key inside free text are found by search.

key.description: The identifier, as written anywhere (case and spacing do not matter).

offset.description: Where the rows start, from the paging line of an earlier call. Default 0.

tools.name: list_fields
description: List every field of a source: its kind, how many documents have it, and its top values.
When to call it: the source list does not show the field you need (it shows only the common ones), or you are unsure of a field's exact name. Give near= words to bring matching names first.
Example: list_fields(source="<source>", near="due date")
What comes back: the source's size and dates, how many fields are near your words, then 50 fields at a time ('fields 1-50 of 607; next: offset=50').

source.description: The source (a name from the source list).

near.description: Words of the field name you look for; the nearest names come first.

offset.description: Where the page starts, from the paging line of an earlier call. Default 0.

tools.name: field_values
description: List the real values of one field of a source, with how many documents hold each.
When to call it: before filtering on a value you are not sure how the records write (a team, a stage, a band), or to see what values exist. Give near= words to bring the closest values first.
Example: field_values(source="<source>", field="<field>", near="sre team")

What comes back: the number of distinct values, how many documents have the field with a value, empty, or not at all, then 50 values at a time with their document counts and other spellings, and a paging line.

source.description: The source (a name from the source list).

field.description: The field, as list_fields or the source list shows it.

near.description: Words of the value you look for; the nearest values come first.

offset.description: Where the page starts, from the paging line of an earlier call. Default 0.

tools.name: finish
description: End the run with your final answer to the question.
When to call it: once, as your last action, when every part of the question is answered, or when you have looked and the documents do not hold what is still missing.
Call it on its own: other tool calls in the same reply are not run.
Example: finish(answer="The launch moved to 12 March because the supplier was late.", citations=["D3", "R1"], not_found=[])
What comes back: 'Answer received.' and the run ends. If an argument is not valid, an error comes back instead; fix it and call finish again.

answer.description: The full answer, in plain sentences, built only from facts that tool results showed. Answer every part of the question. If a part could not be found, say so plainly here too (for example: 'The documents do not say who approved it.'). Never empty.

citations.description: The documents the answer relies on: D# handles, and R# handles for whole result sets (an R# cites every document in it, so cite it when the answer covers the whole set), each exactly as a tool result showed it. Include a document only if it states something the question asks for and the answer uses it; leave out background documents and documents you read while looking. Never invent a handle. Empty when the documents do not contain what the question asks for, even if the answer describes related documents.

not_found.description: Each part of the question the documents do not answer, in a few words (for example: 'who approved the change'). Empty when every part is answered.
